opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few separate reasons, and they're worth pulling apart.

The first is that being better than you on average isn't the same as being a perfect substitute for you. Even if a model writes better code or solves math problems more reliably than I do, I still have to judge whether its output is correct, whether it's solving the right problem, and how it fits into what I'm actually trying to do. You can't evaluate work well in a domain you don't understand. If you've never learned to write a proof, you won't know when the model hands you something that looks like a proof but has a gap in it. So a lot of the value of the skill moves from production to verification and direction, and that still requires you to have learned it.

The second is that skills aren't modular in the way people sometimes imagine. When you learn something like programming or statistics, you're not just acquiring the ability to produce that output. You're changing how you think about other problems. Learning probability changes how you reason about everyday uncertainty. Learning to program changes how you break problems into pieces. Those cognitive side effects don't go away just because a model can now produce the end product more cheaply.

The third is about comparative advantage, which economists keep emphasizing and people keep forgetting. The question isn't whether the AI is better than you in absolute terms, it's what the best allocation of effort is given everyone's capabilities and constraints. AI compute is not infinite and not free, at least for a while. If the model is a thousand times better at one thing and only twice as good at another, it can make sense for humans to keep doing the second thing, and having a broad base of skills makes you more flexible in finding where your comparative advantage actually lies.

And then there's a simpler point: a lot of people learn things because they enjoy them, or because understanding the world is valuable to them for its own sake. Chess engines have been far better than humans for decades, and people still play and study chess. I don't think that's irrational. Understanding something yourself is a different good from having access to an oracle that understands it.

That said, I'd add a caveat. I don't think this lasts forever. As AI systems become more general and more reliable, the verification argument weakens, and the comparative advantage argument becomes less important as compute gets cheaper. So in the long run, I think the case for learning a skill becomes more about intrinsic value and less about economic value. But over the next several years, I think there's still a lot of practical reason to actually learn things rather than just outsource them.

r001.rationale: It says skills transfer across problems and change how a person thinks, and that a broad skill base helps them find where they have an advantage. This communicates value from skills working across domains even when models outperform the person.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says you need to understand a domain to judge whether a model’s output is correct and whether it solves the right problem.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss creative taste or skilled writers using language models to multiply their productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the mistake people make is treating the value of a skill as if it were purely about where you sit in some global ranking of who's best at the task. And that's just not how most of the value of learning things actually gets realized.

So take something like learning to code. Even if a language model can write the code faster and with fewer bugs than I can, the fact that I know how code works changes what I can do with the model. I can tell when it's going wrong, I can ask better questions, I can specify what I actually want at the right level of abstraction, and I can judge whether the output is good. Someone who never learned the skill can't do any of that. They're basically stuck trusting the system blindly, and the gap between those two people is still enormous even if neither of them is writing the code by hand anymore.

There's also a more basic point, which is that skills don't exist in isolation. When you learn something, you're not just acquiring the ability to produce a particular output. You're building up a model of the domain, and that model feeds into everything else you think about. If I learn math, the value isn't mostly that I can compute integrals that a model could compute for me. It's that I now have concepts and intuitions that let me reason about a whole class of problems, including problems where I'm not even going to use the math directly. Models being better at the surface task doesn't take that away from you.

And then I'd add that comparative advantage still matters even when you're worse at everything in absolute terms. Models have finite compute, there are things that are costly to delegate, there's a lot of context that lives in your head that's expensive to transmit. So in practice there's a huge amount of work that it still makes sense for a person to do themselves, even if in principle a machine could do it better. That's been true of human specialization forever. The person who's worse than the expert at everything still ends up doing useful work.

So I'd say the question of whether a skill is worth learning depends much more on how it changes your own capabilities and understanding than on whether you'll ever be the best in the world at it. Almost nobody is the best in the world at anything, and that's never been the reason to learn things.

r001.rationale: It says knowing how code works changes what a person can do with a model, including asking better questions and specifying the task, so the skill remains valuable in combination with model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says domain knowledge lets someone spot when the model is going wrong and judge whether its output is good.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss writers, creative taste, or using language models as productivity multipliers.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think being better than you at something is different from making your knowledge of that thing useless. There are already lots of people who are better programmers than I am, but that doesn’t mean there’s no value in my knowing how to program.

With language models, knowing the subject can help you ask better questions, judge whether an answer makes sense, and decide what to do with it. If you know nothing about programming, you might have trouble telling whether the model has actually built what you wanted. If you understand the problem, you can get much more out of the same model, even if it writes better code than you do.

Now, that argument has limits. If the model can reliably handle the whole process, including figuring out what you want and checking its own work, then the practical value of some skills could fall a lot. But outperforming you at the skill isn’t, by itself, enough to establish that. And there’s also the possibility that you enjoy learning it or want to understand the world better, independently of whether it gives you an economic advantage.

r001.rationale: It says subject knowledge helps a person ask better questions, judge answers, and decide what to do with them, preserving value alongside a stronger model.

r002.rationale: It says knowing the subject helps assess whether an answer makes sense and that someone with no programming knowledge may struggle to tell whether the model built what they wanted.

r003.rationale: It does not mention creative taste, skilled writers, or using language models to multiply writing productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between being better than the model at something and being better at using the model because you understand that thing. Those are quite different. Even if a model is a better programmer than you, knowing how to program can help you ask better questions, evaluate its answers, and understand how a proposed solution fits into what you're trying to do.

And this is a familiar point from economics: you don't need an absolute advantage for your skills to be useful. What matters is the relative cost of doing different things and how you divide up the work. The fact that an AI can do a task better doesn't, by itself, mean that having a human do it has no value.

Now, that doesn't imply every skill will retain its economic value indefinitely. If systems can handle the entire process, including deciding what to do and checking the result, then the argument for learning a particular skill may get weaker. But ‘the model is better at this than I am’ is a much lower bar than ‘learning this no longer helps me.’ And, of course, you might also learn something because you enjoy it or want to understand the world.

r001.rationale: It says understanding a skill can help someone use a model better—by asking better questions, evaluating answers, and fitting solutions to their goals—even when the model outperforms them.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says knowing how to program helps a person evaluate the model’s answers.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss creative taste, skilled writers, or using language models as productivity multipliers.
